headline: Kenya's second Ebola death. Nine cases, one cluster.
summary: A woman of 65 has died of Ebola in Kenya, the second death in the country's first outbreak. She was a close relative of the first patient, a man who fell ill in DR Congo and died in Nairobi on October 5. She was in quarantine when she got sick. Seven more are in isolation: three relatives, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
cover_answer: It kept her from passing it on. It could not save her.
table_question: If a rule protected everyone but you, would you still follow it?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Kenya, a country in Africa, a few people have caught a very bad germ called Ebola. Doctors are keeping everyone who was near them in a special hospital so the germ can't jump to anyone else, like a lid on a pot. It is far from here, and the grown-ups there know what to do. Washing your hands does the same job at home.
5-7.why: A lid on a pot is the whole idea. The deaths can wait for a question.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid detail for the whole story and reads your face before your words, so the script gives them one picture, the lid on the pot, and leaves the deaths out unless they ask. Cantor found this age fears harm it can picture, so the germ stays behind a hospital door. Expect "can I catch it?" The answer is no.

8-12.script: A man with Ebola travelled from Congo to Nairobi and died on October 5. It passes by touching a sick person's blood or vomit, so everyone close to him went into quarantine. One relative, 65, got sick anyway and has died. Quarantine is a fence around whoever might be next: if one gets sick, it stops there.
8-12.why: Sick man, contacts fenced in, one falls ill, nobody outside.
8-12.why_long: At this age a child builds chains of cause and effect and checks whether the rule did what it promised, so the script runs the chain in order: the man, the contacts, the one who fell ill, the zero outside. The fence is the mechanism, and a death inside it is the fence doing its job. Expect "so it didn't work?" Say what it was for.

13-17.script: If someone in quarantine dies anyway, did the quarantine fail? Kenya's second Ebola death was a woman of 65, isolated as a contact of the first patient, her relative. Nobody outside that cluster has caught it. Second: the US told Americans not to travel to Kenya at all. Nine cases, one cluster. Proportionate?
13-17.why: Two true things: she died, and the fence held. Then a judgement call.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the woman died in quarantine, and the quarantine did its job. The script hands them that pair, then a judgement call, a travel warning for a whole country over nine cases in one cluster. Kuhn's point: arguing well is practised, and it needs an honest partner. Expect "what would you do?" Answer it.

5-7.a: No. It is in Kenya, very far away, and it only passes by touching a very sick person's blood or vomit. Here, washing your hands is plenty.

8-12.q: Why did she get sick in quarantine?
8-12.a: She caught it before quarantine began. It stopped her spreading it.
Bundibugyo Ebola has no approved vaccine yet. Trials are under way.

13-17.a: It kept her from passing it on. Nobody outside the cluster is sick.

13-17.q: Why no vaccine for this kind?
13-17.a: Bundibugyo is a rare species. No approved vaccine; trials are under way.
